This paper introduces the TVP-AR($p$) model, a flexible time-series model capable of capturing both linear and nonlinear temporal dependencies through its time-varying autoregressive coefficients. We demonstrate that maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) yields consistent and asymptotically normal coefficient estimates. Furthermore, a novel smoothing procedure is proposed to recover the functional forms of these time-varying coefficients from the discrete MLE results. The analytical framework is applied to investigate the R\&D investment function and the newness function. Empirical findings indicate that firms selectively invest in R\&D to stimulate product innovation and develop novel outputs. Additionally, we observe a U-shaped relationship between recent past sales and the coefficient associated with R\&D investment one period prior, suggesting that companies with lower recent sales tend to increase R\&D spending, whereas those with higher recent sales may decrease it. To investigate potential structural changes in this function post-pandemic, we generalize the model to a piecewise constant coefficient variant. The results reveal a statistically significant shift in the intercept of the R\&D investment function following pandemic-related restrictions. A simplified version of this generalized model is also employed as a dynamic prior in Bayesian optimization efforts aimed at boosting R\&D investment and associated product novelty after lockdown measures are lifted. Supplementary materials provide further details on the empirical analysis and contain additional empirical results, theoretical proofs, and further discussions on optimization.

Although the concept of employing stellar photometry to monitor the atmosphere for high-energy astrophysics optical experiments appears simple, achieving the high precision required to determine vertical aerosol optical depth (VAOD) to within 0.01 has been challenging. Wide-field photometry spanning various altitudes enables a rapid, calibration-independent VAOD calculation, while simultaneously serving as a valuable calibration by-product. By leveraging multi-year datasets from the FRAM (F/(Ph)otometric Robotic Atmospheric Monitor) telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory in Argentina and approximately one year of data from a comparable instrument at the future Cherenkov Telescope Array site in Chile, we have refined measurement techniques to enhance precision, potentially surpassing the 0.01 threshold. Crucially, this analysis relied on detailed laboratory assessments of the system's response to light spectrum and intensity, as the standard assumption of CCD detector linearity no longer holds under these specific observational conditions. Looking ahead, applying these methods to other telescopes equipped with imaging photometric systems could generate extensive calibration datasets, thereby supporting the calibration of airborne and space-based optical experiments. Such efforts are particularly relevant for atmospheric correction in astrophotometry and for calibrating spaceborne radiometers designed for climate monitoring. In this work, we detail the application of this technique at the site future high-energy telescope array, outlining necessary adaptations for its specialized instruments, and we establish a chain of inter-comparisons among multiple calibration methods used for the array's detectors. Furthermore, we present recent progress in directly validating the vertical aerosol optical depth values derived from stellar photometry using independent side-pulse lidar measurements. Ultimately, future calibration of the channel detectors at the site array will be performed utilizing this same approach.

This study evaluates and compares numerous numerical techniques for addressing stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics, which rely on combinations of deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. Leveraging recent work by the authors, the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion is employed to analyze sampling accuracy and quantify stepsize-dependent biases in configurational averaging. For harmonic oscillators, specific schemes yield exact configurational averaging, potentially enhancing the modeling of biomolecules where bond stretching is critical. In general systems, an optimal method is identified that exhibits significantly lower bias than alternatives. Simulations of the alanine dipeptide (both solvated and unsolvated) demonstrate that this approach achieves higher accuracy without sacrificing computational efficiency, supports larger timesteps, and maintains the conformational exploration rate. The proposed scheme represents a uniformly superior algorithm for molecular sampling, offering practical timestep increases of over 25% in vacuum and reducing errors in configurational averages by more than a factor of ten in solvated simulations at large timesteps. These improvements are particularly advantageous for free energy calculations and other applications demanding high precision, such as refining force fields. Current automatic image description models are typically trained and assessed using crowdsourced human-generated captions, with system performance measured by similarity metrics such as BLEU, Meteor, and CIDER. Consequently, the reliability of both the systems and their evaluation hinges on the quality of these reference descriptions. As demonstrated in Section 2, existing image description datasets lack sufficient quality. I contend that more detailed guidelines are necessary, ones that balance the specific requirements of visually impaired users with the practical feasibility of generating appropriate descriptions. While high-quality data would allow for reference-based evaluation, we should also explore alternative assessment methods. These alternatives could enable the scoring of more permissive descriptions suited to real-world scenarios where creating detailed accounts of every image is often unrealistic. Furthermore, such approaches would facilitate the evaluation of "rough draft" generating models. This paper examines the necessary qualities of image description data, analyzes current datasets against these standards, and proposes potential strategies for acquiring higher-quality references.

Quantifying complexity within quantum field theory remains a formidable challenge, primarily due to the difficulty of moving past free models and their associated Gaussian states and operations. Our approach addresses this by examining conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, offering a comprehensive analysis of complexity for both states and operators within the universal sector of their energy-momentum tensor. Central to our framework are the Euler-Arnold equations and their integro-differential extensions, which ensure the optimization problem between arbitrary states or transformations is well-defined. This work expands upon the findings detailed in arXiv:2001.09680 and arXiv:2001.09679. As highlighted by the title of this article, our investigation yields a result that appears to contradict the holographic bound, a phenomenon linked to the infrared divergence arising from integrating over optimal circuits that deviate from geodesic paths. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the rate of growth in state complexity for 1+1 dimensional conformal field theories strictly depends on their central charge. Specifically, the rate is zero when $c=1$, follows a quadratic progression for $1<c\leqslant 2$, and exhibits linear growth for central charges exceeding 2. These conclusions were achieved by solving the Euler-Arnold equations (and their integro-differential forms) specific to each individual central charge. Our study confirms that, contrary to expectations, 1+1 dimensional conformal field theories with $c>2$ can exceed the holographic bound of seven. This violation implies that such theories cannot be described by an asymptotically AdS5 gravitational dual, thereby restricting the realizability of 1+1 dimensional conformal field theories with $c>7$ through holographic mechanisms. Along the way, we also established several mathematical properties of the solution to these equations, properties that may prove valuable in other mathematical contexts. The Euler-Arnold equations themselves represent an intriguing subject of investigation, potentially significant for various areas of research, including quantum information theory. Our work provides additional mathematical details regarding these equations to support future studies in this domain. The framework developed here opens possibilities for analyzing further 1+1 dimensional field theories, although this extends beyond the scope of the current paper. Notably, our method could potentially be applied to free theories, although we do not pursue this direction in our research. We thank the community for their interest. This research conducts a linear analysis of a turbulent methane-air jet flame to forecast how the reacting flow responds to upstream acoustic actuation. Within a linearized framework, capturing heat release fluctuations is essential for studying thermoacoustic instabilities and flame noise. Distinct from prior work, this investigation employs an active flame methodology, which incorporates heat release oscillations induced by acoustic fluctuations. Implementing this approach linearly requires linearizing a combustion model around a base state composed of acoustically excited turbulent jets. Crucially, the proposed method does not rely on Fourier mode decomposition; instead, it allows for the examination of flame response spatial distributions to identify local instabilities, such as swirling vortex instabilities, within linearly acoustic actuated jets. Comparing the results with Direct Numerical Simulations of acoustically forced turbulent jets reveals that the linearized model accurately predicts response amplitudes for acoustic modes and other spatial modes with significant axial velocity alignment. Furthermore, the model successfully accounts for the generation of Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities when the actuation Mach number is high. The linearized combustion model serves as a valuable tool for analyzing direct numerical simulations of acoustically forced turbulent jets and can support reduced-order modeling within the context of active flame control.

Nonlocal gravity (NLG) represents a classical, nonlocal extension of Einstein's gravitational theory, modeled after the analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics in media. Within this framework, historical dependence is introduced through a constitutive relation that utilizes a causal kernel, which must ultimately be derived from observational data. This paper aims to reformulate nonlocal gravity so that the nonlocal components of the constitutive relation directly link measurable quantities, mirroring the approach found in nonlocal electrodynamics. The derived constitutive relation aligns with a recent proposal by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl [25]. Utilizing this updated constitutive relation for nonlocal gravity, it is demonstrated that de Sitter spacetime does not constitute a valid solution. Furthermore, when applied to linear de Sitter-like constitutive relations, the reformulated theory contradicts observational data, offering a more stringent test than previous formulations of nonlocal gravity. The goal of this research is to facilitate the development of constitutive relations capable of describing gravitational nonlocality observed in cosmic-scale phenomena. This work serves as a continuation of a project aiming to explore whether the constitutive relation can reveal nonlocal behavior in a classical, causal gravitational model that otherwise retains the mathematical structure of general relativity. Such an endeavor could provide a classical, nonlocal alternative to quantum gravity that is mathematically equivalent to general relativity (or its teleparallel equivalent), potentially offering a unified theoretical framework to explain quantum-like nonlocality in gravitational wave experiments and other cosmic nonlocal observations. In this project, it is assumed that the constitutive relation is local in a causal, rational functional form suitable for implementation on supercomputers to handle the required high-dimensional calculations. Additionally, the constitutive relation should ideally remain stable under variations in the nonlocal variable, representing a form of "robust nonlocality," although this is not strictly necessary. As noted by a colleague, "classical nonlocality is an oddity," and indeed, the concept of a nonlocal variable itself remains a subject of debate. In this project, the nonlocal variable is defined as a causal operator acting on a causal kernel, a definition that may prove useful in investigating classical nonlocality. It is important to emphasize, however, that this paper does not attempt to justify the legitimacy of this definition or the overall research program; such justifications will be addressed in future publications. The detection of certain variable X-ray sources in the Galactic Centre that have not exhibited outbursts over a ten-year monitoring period has led to the hypothesis of a substantial population of stellar-mass black holes in this area. A fundamental premise of this argument is the assertion that neutron stars in low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) do not experience long intervals between transients. However, this paper demonstrates that approximately half of the known transient LMXBs with confirmed neutron star primaries exhibit recurrence times exceeding a decade when observed with MAXI sensitivity. Furthermore, we show that to align the expected total number of neutron star LMXBs with both current observations and the galaxy's millisecond radio pulsar population, the dominant class of these systems must have recurrence times far surpassing a century for MAXI-detectable outbursts, implying that few such systems have been identified to date. These findings indicate that existing neutron star LMXB data can account for all millisecond pulsar LMXB observations without necessitating the introduction of additional black hole systems.

Bipartite graphs represent the connections between two separate sets of entities. These structures are frequently depicted in a two-tiered layout, where each entity set is shown as a collection of vertices aligned on one of two parallel horizontal lines, and their relationships are illustrated by edges linking corresponding vertices across the lines. A primary goal in creating such visualizations is to reduce edge crossings, ideally achieving zero crossings to produce planar drawings, though this is often impossible. Consequently, minimizing crossings serves as a key strategy for enhancing readability. This paper introduces a refined algorithm that finds a planar bipartite drawing with at most $k$ crossings, ensuring edges remain straight and vertices stay on two parallel lines, while also avoiding crossings on the lines themselves. For a genuine planar graph $G$, the algorithm's time complexity is $O(2^{72} \cdot n + n^{2})$, where $n$ represents the total number of vertices and $m$ the number of edges in $G$. Given that the complexity is both linear in $n$ and exponential only in $k$, it is reasonable to question whether this limit of 72 exponentiations is optimal. To address this, the authors present additional results aimed at further lowering this exponent. The proposed algorithm has been made accessible via https://github.com/ChandraSekharRavulapati/BiSplit. Keywords: Graph drawing, bipartite graph, edge crossings, vertex splitting, fixed parameter tractability, planarity, and crossing number are associated with this work. Performance degradation techniques serve as a crucial complement to side-channel attacks, enabling the extraction of secret data at speeds unattainable through channels alone. While prior research has predominantly focused on electrical vulnerabilities like cache and simple pipeline speculation attacks, this study introduces a novel method: a performance degradation technique specifically designed to combat simple pipeline speculation attacks. We first demonstrate that standard countermeasures, such as flushing the execution pipeline, can be exploited to create a performance side-channel itself. Leveraging this insight, we present HyperDegrade, a methodology that systematically selects and combines performance degradation attacks to establish a potent side-channel attack. Our findings reveal that this performance side-channel operates approximately 100 times faster than previously possible with simple pipeline attacks. Consequently, we detail a practical attack scenario where an adversary on the same CPU core as the target application successfully extracts a 256-bit master key in under 11 minutes using HyperDegrade. To validate our approach, we implemented HyperDegrade on real hardware, confirming the efficacy of our performance degradation technique and the associated side-channel attack. Furthermore, we examined the broader implications of these performance degradation methods against other side-channel attacks. Although HyperDegrade does not exacerbate simple time-attacks as significantly as it does simple pipeline attacks, we identified a new side-channel attack enabled by these performance degradation methods that surpasses even simple time-attacks in efficacy. Finally, we demonstrated that HyperDegrade remains effective against this attack even when CPUs employ speculative execution mitigation mechanisms. To the best of our knowledge, this work constitutes the first demonstration of a performance degradation technique, the formulation of a corresponding performance side-channel, and the construction of an attack chain leveraging this side-channel to secret data. We conclude by outlining several potential applications of this performance side-channel. Given that performance fluctuations can manifest as measurable power consumption variations, we sketched out an attack combining our performance side-channel with power analysis. Additionally, we proposed integrating this performance side-channel with simple time-attacks as a countermeasure to performance optimization strategies. As performance degradation methods could potentially be utilized as a side-channel against simple time-attacks, we illustrated an attack chain achieving 100x greater extraction speed than a simple time-channel alone. We also highlighted the risk posed by these performance degradation techniques in the context of denial-of-service attacks, noting that they could be more damaging than traditional ones. To mitigate such denial-of-service threats, we proposed countermeasures that could inadvertently leak secret data via our performance side-channel, which an attacker could exploit

An unknotting operation represents a local modification applied to knot diagrams. It is possible to convert any knot diagram into a trivial unknot diagram through a combination of unknotting operations and Reidemeister moves. These operations hold substantial significance in knot theory, particularly for analyzing knot complexity and invariants. Furthermore, they play a crucial role in fields such as biology, chemistry, and physics, where they help investigate the complex entanglements found in strings, organic molecules, and DNA. This paper introduces a novel unknotting operation known as the diagonal move, applicable to both classical and welded knots. We demonstrate that the crossing change, Delta-move, Sharp-move, Gamma-move, n-gon move, pass move, and 4-move can all be achieved via sequences of diagonal moves. Additionally, we define a distance metric based on the diagonal move and examine its characteristics. Our findings indicate that the distance measured using the diagonal move is strictly smaller than those associated with the Delta-move, Crossing change, or n-gon move. To support these conclusions, we provide relevant proofs and tabular data. Visually, the diagonal move involves performing a U-shape twist in a knot diagram along with a corresponding slide adjustment, as illustrated in Figure 1. From the perspective of welded knots, the diagonal move is equivalent to the standard diagonal exchange move used in that context. Finally, we establish that for classical knots, the unknotting move and the diagonal move are equivalent when viewed through the lens of welded knots. These results are of particular importance in the study of classical, virtual, and welded knots. The high-frequency sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors is constrained by quantum shot noise and ultimately by optical losses within the signal-recycling cavity. This limitation represents a primary barrier to detecting gravitational waves from binary neutron star mergers in both current and future detectors. To surpass this limit, a new topological design is essential. This paper evaluates the high-frequency sensitivity of a sloshing Sagnac interferometer (SSI), an architecture previously suggested by the LIGO collaboration to observe a binary black hole collision in the LIGO X observing run. By tracing the spectral density of strain noise across various SSI configurations, we identify an optimal setup and demonstrate that it can exceed the sensitivity of a conventional Lloyd interferometer by a factor of 2.5 at 2.2\,kHz, assuming current loss levels in the signal recycling cavity of the equivalent Lloyd interferometer. Furthermore, we show how varying interferometric losses can be utilized to overcome the Heisenberg limit associated with the signal recycling cavity. Finally, we discuss the practical implementation of this optimal configuration and outline necessary steps to achieve it. (401 words)

Extra-large scale massive multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO) systems represent a promising solution for delivering ultra-high data rates in environments with high user density. Because the physical dimensions of XL-MIMO arrays are comparable to the distances separating them from user equipments (UEs), the system experiences spatial non-stationarities and distinct visibility regions (VRs). These factors, combined with high UE density and limited pilot resources, make the design of random access (RA) protocols and scheduling algorithms particularly difficult. This paper introduces a joint RA and scheduling approach called the non-overlapping VR XL-MIMO (NOVR-XL) protocol. This method leverages the unique VRs of individual UEs to enhance RA performance and prioritizes scheduling UEs with non-overlapping VRs within the same payload data pilot resource. Simulation results demonstrate that this proposed scheme yields substantial improvements in sum rate compared to conventional RA methods, while also lowering access latency and overall connectivity performance. The source of these gains lies in the system's ability to process UEs with non-overlapping VRs in parallel and optimizing the use of pilot resources. Furthermore, we derive analytical expressions for sum rate, mean access delay, and connectivity probability, which are validated against simulation data. Finally, the study provides insights into how sum rate, access delay, and connectivity probability are influenced by various system parameters.

Although neural language models have largely replaced traditional $N$-gram models due to superior performance, our findings suggest that $N$-grams still yield better results in specific scenarios, such as out-of-domain prediction and certain evaluation tasks like meta-test metrics. These outcomes highlight the difficulty of fully supplanting $N$-grams with neural approaches. This paper introduces a hybrid architecture where a neural language model learns residuals from an $N$-gram model, enabling the neural component to focus on capturing contextual linguistic details beyond $N$-grams. Our experiments demonstrate that this hybrid model outperforms existing state-of-the-art language models across various tasks and datasets. Additionally, the $N$-gram residual learning framework is applicable to other domains where traditional models are used, including acoustics and vision. Code is accessible at: https://github.com/lingdust/Brownian.

This study investigates the performance of Informed OCR (iOCR), a system developed to correct errors in conventional OCR for vote tabulation using a spell correction algorithm. The findings indicate that iOCR outperforms traditional OCR methods. Additionally, the spell correction algorithm successfully identified and fixed errors in previously unrecognized printed candidate names and minor mark-sense misreads, thereby enhancing overall accuracy. These results confirm that iOCR is highly effective for ballot processing and related applications. Furthermore, this work introduces an open-source toolkit named BallotRec, which enables researchers to evaluate the precision of any OCR or iOCR toolkit on specific ballot datasets. This study investigates potential global atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere using a simplified General Circulation Model (GCM) derived from the University of Hamburg's Portable University Model for the Atmosphere. The model incorporates simplified representations of solar and terrestrial heating, surface friction, and land-ocean contrasts, while explicitly including Coriolis and centrifugal forces but omitting other physical processes. By systematically varying the intensity of terrestrial heating and surface friction across 30 simulations, the authors performed a comparative analysis using vertical cross-sections of zonal winds, meridional circulation cells, and eddy kinetic energy, supplemented by other diagnostic tools. Their findings indicate that three primary circulation regimes form depending primarily on the balance between direct and indirect thermal driving forces: a super-rotational regime, a transitional regime, and a geostrophic regime characterized by turbulent flow. These results align with previous discoveries from other simplified GCMs and real-world observations, underscoring the significance of surface friction and centrifugal forces in the context of terrestrial and exoplanetary atmospheres that exhibit substantial equator-to-pole temperature gradients. Additionally, the identified circulation regimes in this GCM share similarities with those observed in gas giant atmospheres, which lack solid surfaces and experience negligible friction, primarily due to the dominance of baroclinic and barotropic instabilities in the latter. Ultimately, these circulation regimes are universal phenomena driven by fundamental forces and boundary conditions, applicable to both planetary atmospheres with surfaces and gas giant atmospheres. Furthermore, these patterns may offer valuable insights for interpreting global flow patterns on ExoPlanets, particularly when assessing the feasibility of habitability. The three dominant regimes—the geostrophic turbulent regime, the super-rotational regime, and an intermediate transitional regime—mirror instability patterns seen in fluid dynamics laboratory experiments and are also relevant to molten iron cores. As key fingerprints of boundary conditions and fundamental forces, these regimes can guide future explorations of global flow patterns in exotic environments, such as the atmospheres of brown dwarfs and white dwarfs. To comprehensively examine the causes, characteristics, and stability of these primary regimes and their associated patterns (such as wave-like structures and circulation cells) across varying boundary conditions and fundamental forces, this paper focuses on a detailed examination of these phenomena under specific configurations of surface friction and cooling intensities. Ultimately, these investigations will facilitate the adaptation of these patterns for analyzing the global flow patterns of ExoPlanets in upcoming operational atmospheric Re-construction models designed for Habitability assessments and ExoPlanet detection initiatives. This study presents a real integral formulation for the reciprocal $\Gamma$ function using a regularized hypersingular integral. It confirms the equivalence between this new form and the standard complex representation, subsequently deriving a regularized complex expression that follows the conventional Hankel contour. The approach is extended to generalized orders, where a regularized complex formula is derived for the product of a fractional power $z^{-\alpha}$ and a reciprocal Gamma function $\Gamma(\alpha + z)^{-1}$. This generalization is applied to derive a regularized real integral representation for the product of a fractional power $x^{-\alpha}$ and a Bessel function $J_{\nu}(x)$. Finally, a corresponding regularized real integral representation is obtained for the product of $x^{\alpha -1}$ and the modified Bessel function $K_{\nu}(x)$. The significance of these regularized representations lies in their utility for numerically computing these products when arguments are small, and in facilitating asymptotic expansions via iterated integration by parts. These theoretical developments are demonstrated through specific examples.

While Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) excel at addressing large-scale problems across numerous domains, their deployment in real-time systems is often hindered by the sheer volume of parameters involved. To overcome this challenge, Teacher-Student architectures were initially introduced in the context of knowledge distillation, enabling lightweight student networks to match the performance of complex teacher models. Recently, these architectures have been widely adopted for diverse knowledge learning tasks, including knowledge distillation, expansion, adaptation, and multi-task learning. Leveraging such frameworks, recent research has successfully achieved multiple learning objectives through efficient and compact student networks. Unlike previous surveys focused solely on knowledge distillation, this review comprehensively examines various Teacher-Student architectures across a spectrum of knowledge learning goals. Furthermore, we systematically analyze strategies for optimizing student networks, the construction of representative knowledge in teacher networks, and the regulatory mechanisms governing both architectures. Finally, we discuss open issues and potential future research directions regarding these architectures and strategies. By providing a thorough survey of Teacher-Student architectures across different knowledge learning objectives, this work offers valuable insights for industry applications and guides future academic investigations. The accompanying table summarizes the key Teacher-Student architectures reviewed in this survey. Leveraging deterministic finite state automata, we integrate this concise representation into Bucket Elimination (BE), a general variable elimination method used for inference and optimization problems like most probable explanation and constrained optimization. We refer to this enhanced approach as FABE. Incorporating our compact representation into FABE significantly enhances BE's performance regarding both runtime and memory usage. Specifically, when applied to the formal verification of AI systems through most probable explanation, our method identifies certain first-order logic goals that remain computationally intractable for existing techniques. Furthermore, we seamlessly integrate our representation and FABE into backtracking-based solvers for constrained satisfaction problems, yielding additional runtime improvements in this domain as well. Significance testing, particularly the paired-permutation test, has been essential for ensuring that performance differences between NLP systems are statistically significant rather than due to chance. However, practitioners have historically relied on Monte Carlo approximations because no suitable exact algorithm existed. This paper introduces an efficient exact algorithm for the paired-permutation test applicable to a specific family of structured test statistics. The proposed algorithm operates in $O(N^2)$ time, where $N$ represents the total number of data points. Although restricted to certain test statistics, this approach represents the first exact method capable of handling Aspects or Word2Vec similarities. Implemented as open-source code, our solution surpasses Monte Carlo variants in both speed and accuracy. Additionally, we establish a new upper bound for the complexity of computing exact p-values with any regression-based significance test. Our code is available at https://github.com/abhinavw99/ExactPairedPermutationTesting.

This study presents a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter that models target birth and undetected target intensities on a grid. It employs a simplified Rao-Blackwellized point mass filter to predict undetected target intensities and approximates the density of newly born targets. Unlike traditional approaches that render PMBM prior intensity parameters intractable, this method keeps them tractable and constant. Additionally, it handles target detections across multiple sensor types with varying ranges and probabilities of detection. Simulations demonstrate that the proposed method achieves higher trace of the Cramer-Rao lower bound (CRLB) coverage compared to conventional PMBM filters. These simulations also illustrate the impact of prior intensity parameters on filter performance and confirm that the proposed approach outperforms competitors when sensor detection probabilities are low. Finally, the simulations validate the rapid convergence of PMBM prior parameter estimates to true values using unscented particle updates. The practical utility of these estimates is explored through a sensor scheduling application. Real data simulations based on an air defense scenario involving radar and infrared sensors show that the method optimizes air asset utilization by leveraging multi-sensor detections and undetected target estimates. Soccer is a game characterized by sparse rewards, where even minor errors can result in goals conceded. Although soccer matches are fundamentally zero-sum in nature, teams operate with distinct objectives: avoiding defeat takes precedence over scoring, and securing a draw is preferable to losing. Consequently, during critical moments, teams may adopt risk-averse strategies, prioritizing goal conservation over offensive advancement. This study introduces a novel state-space augmented deep deterministic dynamic programming approach, combined with value iteration, specifically designed for soccer. We formulate the problem as a Markov decision process and apply a reward function that varies based on the game state. Initially, we analyze the data distribution across a market of professional soccer teams in Japan's J-League. Subsequently, we train artificial intelligence agents to generate near-optimal policies for this distribution. These agents are then pitted against one another in simulated games. Furthermore, we specifically train agents to make optimal decisions when their teams face defeat or trailing scores. The results indicate that in simulated contests where an agent's team was losing or behind, the policy optimized for these specific states outperformed the overall default policy. Once leading or tied, the agents reverted to their global optimal policy. These findings suggest that decomposing the state-space to derive policies tailored for situations of defeat or deficit is more effective than training agents solely on the game's raw data distribution. Additionally, these results support the conclusion that deep reinforcement learning methods, such as those used by FIFA World Cup teams like Germany and France, can be further improved. Finally, this research holds significant value for soccer betting applications. The source code and data required to reproduce these results are accessible at: https://github.com/Abhishek-1908/SOCCO.

Driven by the unprecedented rise in telework and remote learning demands, there is an increasing call for enabling scientists and engineers to control complex experiments via the internet without direct physical presence. While automated data collection and visualization are now commonplace, facilitating the remote adjustment of experimental parameters to explore different operating conditions remains a significant challenge. Laser Doppler Vibrometry (LDV) represents a high-cost, high-precision non-contact measurement technique ideally suited for automation. This report details the development of a system capable of acquiring 2D vibration maps using a single probe point LDV, guided by a pre-recorded laser trace. We demonstrate that this approach yields accurate results when applied to simple vibration modes, though challenges persist with complex mode shapes. Furthermore, we highlight how this setup can facilitate the rapid screening of large areas to identify optimal locations for single or multi-point configurations for more detailed investigations. Beyond its immediate utility for LDV applications, this concept offers a versatile blueprint for remotely guiding other single-point non-contact measurement systems to map out areas of interest.

Finally, we establish the explicit formulation of a virial identity applicable to time-dependent solitary wave solutions.

The masses and spins of black holes powering Active Galactic Nuclei (AGNs) and producing jets can be investigated through their electromagnetic spectra. We employ the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear relationship linking four source-frame variables: radio luminosity, X-ray or optical luminosity (derived from the [OIII] emission line), black hole mass, and spin. By incorporating uncertainties related to luminosity measurements, conversion factors, relativistic beaming, and AGN physical properties, we establish lower limits on the spins of a sample of massive, jetted AGNs. Utilizing these findings, we examine the direct consequences for the mass spectrum of ultra-light scalar, vector, and axial-vector particles (manifesting as axion-like, dark photons, and other hidden photon models) via the superradiance mechanism. Furthermore, comparing these constraints with those from gravitational waves from binary black hole mergers and from primordial black hole evaporation (if applicable), we identify significant implications for the existence of axion-like particle mass gaps and for the hypothesis that all dark matter consists of a single ultralight boson species. Applying these spin limits also allows us to reassess mass limits derived from self-sustaining magnetar stars and from the stability of massive neutron stars, as well as from the survival of strange quark stars. Our limit-setting analysis relies on a sample of 30 massive, jetted AGNs for which data on radio luminosity and at least one proxy for central engine luminosity are available; given the sample size, we emphasize that future investigations with broader samples and with precise spin determinations from X-ray timing spectroscopy or from the $g_{\rm eff}$ metric (when feasible) could yield striking results. Our work underscores the potential utility of analyzing the four fundamental plane variables—even when spin measurements are not yet possible—for constraining the properties of primordial black holes, axion-like particles, and other beyond-Standard-Model physics. The prior assumptions underpinning our limit calculations are detailed, and we provide a table listing all derived axion-like particle mass limits for our sample. Ultimately, integrating limit-setting frameworks based on superradiance, self-gravity, self-sustaining magnetars, and the stability of massive neutron stars or strange quark stars, we identify specific parameters ranges where our constraints are particularly stringent. We simulated the ground states of quantum harmonic oscillators subjected to either constant forces of varying magnitudes or time-dependent driving forces. Expectation values of position were computed for different combinations of mass, natural angular frequency, and the coupling constant $\lambda$ under both driving conditions. Under constant forcing, the simulations yielded coherent states. The outcomes for both scenarios align almost perfectly with theoretical predictions. To perform these simulations, we implemented the Metropolis algorithm on a discrete time lattice to evaluate the systems' imaginary time path integrals. This implementation constitutes a discrete-time Markov chain Monte Carlo method, which, when applied to ground state simulations of quantum systems, is equivalent to a classical classical statistical mechanical system in one higher dimension. This equivalence allows the use of established techniques from classical statistical mechanics to address quantum problems. While this paper focuses on one-dimensional systems, the same approach extends to higher dimensions. Given the growing recognition that many real-world systems exhibit quantum behavior under specific circumstances, this method offers significant potential for investigating such realistic quantum systems. Furthermore, this technique holds promise for analyzing one-dimensional classical statistical mechanical systems with significant applications, including certain aspects of seismology, geology, and materials science. Although this method is particularly effective for ground state simulations, it also holds value for systems governed by semi-classical laws. However, alternative approaches are generally required for time-dependent simulations, as this specific method is not ideally suited for that purpose. Nevertheless, under certain conditions, it can also be utilized for time-dependent scenarios. Ultimately, the widespread adoption of this method could provide a powerful tool for exploring both classical quantum and statistical mechanical systems with practical relevance. We introduce a variant of the quantum relational Hoare logic from Unruh (POPL 2019) that incorporates "expectations" into pre- and postconditions. Specifically, when reasoning about pairs of programs, this logic enables quantitative analysis of the degree to which pre- and postconditions regarding the relationship between program inputs and outputs are satisfied. Unlike Unruh's framework, which required separate assertions for classical and quantum predicates, our approach leverages the fact that quantum predicates are inherently represented as Hermitian operators, which contain both classical and quantum information. Utilizing this logic, we formally validate an optimizer for Q\# that employs two quantum programs to define a distance metric between density matrices, thereby establishing the validity of distance metric optimizers in general. Furthermore, we apply this logic to validate a method by Kaib and Wadler (LCPS 2020) for composing correctness proofs for quantum programs using similarity relations instead of standard predicates. Validations of these meta-level systems were conducted via the Cerberus proof assistant, an extension of Coq developed by the author, where the necessary library for handling Hermitian operators was also created. While this paper focuses on presentations of validations for the aforementioned optimizations and meta-level systems, future work will explore practical applications of the logic for verifying quantum programs through a methodology that involves specifying two versions of a predicate. It remains uncertain if bulge expansion causes the flattening of the star-forming main sequence (MS) at high masses. To examine how bulges influence the MS, we analyzed the NUV$-r$ color—a reliable tracer of specific star formation rate—in the central ($r<R_{50}$) versus outer regions of 6,387 local star-forming galaxies. Our results show that for galaxies with $M_{\ast}<10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, the central NUV$-r$ is only about 0.25 magnitudes redder than the outer regions. However, above $M_{\ast}=10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, the central NUV$-r$ becomes significantly redder than the outer regions, indicating that bulges in massive galaxies are more evolved. When sorting galaxies by S\'ersic index $n$, those with $n>2.5$ exhibit redder central NUV$-r$ colors than those with $n<2.5$, regardless of whether they are classified as classical bulges ($n\geq3$) or pseudobulges ($n<3$). This suggests that the traditional division between classical and pseudo-bulges based on morphology or $n$ does not accurately reflect differences in specific star formation rate between central bulgy and non-bulgy galaxies. Furthermore, the fraction of galaxies with $s$Sersic$>2.5$ rises sharply with mass, accounting for 9%, 25%, and 45% of samples at $M_{\ast}=10^{10.2}$, $10^{10.5}$, and $10^{10.8}M_{\sun}$, respectively. This increase in the $s$Sersic$>2.5$ fraction with mass aligns with the turnover in the MS at log($M_{\ast}/M_{\sun}$)$\sim10.2$10.5 depending on slope, implying that bulge expansion at high masses drives the flattening of the $M_{\ast}$$-$SFR relation. Consequently, future studies of the MS should explicitly consider the mass concentration of galaxies. Simply using aperture-matched or surface-brightness-matched outer regions may introduce biases, as the most massive galaxies already possess highly concentrated starlight in their centers that requires careful handling.

Golay complementary matrices (GCM) have recently attracted significant attention due to their potential applications in omnidirectional precoding. In this paper, we extend GCMs to multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays (GCA) and introduce new construction methods for GCA pairs and quads. These constructions are enabled by a set of identities defined over a commutative ring. We demonstrate the feasibility of these quaternary GCA identities by establishing equivalent identities on the unsimplified Discrete Golay Transform (u-DGT). Utilizing this equivalence, we derive numerous Golay complementary sequence (GCX) pairs and quads, which are then integrated into the new GCA pair and quad construction frameworks. Specifically, we construct a pair of 3-D GCM matrices and two quads of 4-D GCM matrices, alongside several examples of 5-D GCA quads. Finally, we construct a pair of 6-D GCA quads, which represents the highest dimension achieved to date. The practical utility of these constructions is illustrated through the design of optimized omnidirectional DCX and QDCX precoding protocols. Simulation results confirm that these protocols achieve ideal complementary array characteristics and significantly reduce out-of-band leakage compared to existing omnidirectional Asperlin-Golay precoding methods. These findings indicate that the proposed constructions of Golay complementary arrays can be effectively applied in realistic scenarios. Laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) represents a new minimally invasive approach for ablating intracranial structures to manage mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE). While deep learning methods, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), represent the current standard for ROI segmentation, they depend heavily on extensive annotated datasets, which are difficult to gather for emerging procedures like LITT. To address this limitation, we introduce a Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis Framework (PAVAE) designed to increase both the volume and variety of training data. This framework comprises two sequential networks: a mask synthesis network and a mask-guided lesion synthesis network. To leverage extrinsic information for enhanced supervision, we developed a condition embedding block (CEB) and a mask embedding block (MEB) that encode intrinsic mask characteristics into the feature space. Ultimately, a segmentation network was trained on a combination of raw and synthetic lesion images to assess the framework's efficacy. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our approach generates realistic synthetic images and significantly improves the performance of downstream segmentation tasks compared to conventional data augmentation methods. This study tackles the persistent challenge of extracting dynamical information from noisy acoustic emission signals generated by an adhesive tape being peeled under a constant traction velocity. While most existing literature assumes static triggers with fixed locations and patterns—properties upon which many detection mechanisms rely—recent studies have demonstrated that image classification countermeasures like Neural Cleanse and ABS can be circumvented using dynamic triggers that remain effective regardless of their position or appearance. However, such dynamic backdoors are resource-intensive, typically requiring a significant portion of poisoned training data. This work presents the first demonstration that dynamic backdoor attacks can occur via a global average pooling layer without needing an increased volume of poisoned data. Despite this theoretical possibility, experimental results across sound classification, text sentiment analysis, and image classification indicate that implementing such attacks remains highly challenging in practice. Given the severity of a successful dynamic backdoor, these findings highlight the difficulty of detecting and preventing it during actual deployments. Ultimately, our results underscore the value of assuming the presence of dynamic backdoors when defending against them and advocate for further research into mitigating this severe threat. This work addresses the challenge of a Parameter Server (PS) learning a model from data distributed across graph nodes, with Federated Learning (FL) serving as the primary application. A significant hurdle in FL is the communication bottleneck between nodes and the PS. Although performing multiple local updates per iteration before syncing with the PS is a common strategy to alleviate this bottleneck, the statistical heterogeneity of node-specific data often results in biased models and slow convergence. To overcome both communication and data heterogeneity issues, we investigate Random Walk Learning (RWL), where models are exchanged directly between data nodes rather than solely communicating with the PS. Leveraging a mean-field theory, we derive a closed-form expression for the convergence rate under RWL and compare it with the rate achievable via multiple local updates in a standard FL setup. Our analysis indicates that while RWL offers an advantage over multiple local updates when data heterogeneity is high, the benefit diminishes as communication costs rise. Based on this theoretical framework, we design an optimal RWL strategy. Applying this approach to a vertical video recommendation scenario, we observe significant performance gains. Furthermore, in the context of FL, we derive a convergence rate bound for a practical, optimized scheduling policy that accounts for node degrees and iteration-specific learning rates. Numerical experiments validate these bounds and demonstrate that our proposed policies outperform existing methods. Finally, we establish an end-to-end theoretical lower bound for any iterative learning algorithm and introduce two algorithms designed to surpass it; simulation results confirm that our algorithms closely approach this limit. All code and data will be made publicly available at https://github.com/rajatgupta20/WRL_FSL_. We conclude with directions for future research.

Although the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) with advanced information technology systems has delivered substantial benefits to Internet of Vehicles (IoV) ecosystems, it has simultaneously amplified security and privacy risks. Consequently, privacy preservation methods and IoV protocols have gained significant traction among researchers and industry practitioners. However, the rapid proliferation of potential solutions has created challenges in evaluating their relative merits for specific IoV scenarios. Recently, Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a promising approach for data analysis and decision-making within IoV contexts. Concurrently, blockchain technology has attracted considerable attention due to its potential in security management and other applications alongside data processing. Nevertheless, the adoption of both FL and blockchain in IoV remains nascent, leaving many critical issues unresolved. This study provides a comprehensive survey on utilizing FL, blockchain, and their hybrid frameworks for privacy preservation, security, and management within IoV. Additionally, it outlines the necessary components and architectures for implementing these technologies in IoV scenarios. The survey examines various FL algorithms, data management strategies, and protocols required for their operation alongside blockchains and hybrid models. It also categorizes existing solutions based on underlying technologies, potential applications, and key characteristics. Ultimately, this work proposes a novel framework for integrating these technologies into IoV environments, identifies current research gaps, and suggests future directions for developing advanced FL, blockchain, and hybrid systems for data processing, security, and other tasks in IoV. Although this comprehensive survey focuses on specific technologies, approaches, and frameworks for privacy, security, and management in IoV, its detailed analysis of current research trends, methodologies, and limitations will guide future investigations in this domain. Specifically, the proposed framework will assist in addressing remaining challenges and gaps to realize intelligent, secure, and efficient connectivity, data processing, and decision-making within IoV ecosystems. This survey is organized as follows: Section 2 introduces fundamental concepts regarding IoV, Section 3 covers IoT and data processing mechanisms, Section 4 details FL mechanisms and architectures, Section 5 describes blockchain mechanisms and architectures, Section 6 explores FL and blockchain applications in IoV, Section 7 presents a literature review on related topics, Sections 8 and 9 propose frameworks and conclude with future directions respectively, and finally, Appendix A provides definitions for acronyms and terms used throughout this survey. Long-tail networks, characterized by extensive layers and high dimensionality, represent a significant hurdle in deploying recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for video analysis. Although LSTM architectures are theoretically ideal for handling variable-length videos, their practical application is constrained by substantial memory requirements and computationally heavy operations. This study introduces both algorithmic and hardware designs for a streamlined, energy-efficient LSTM network tailored for video recognition tasks. Our algorithmic strategy utilizes a space-time restructuring approach combined with a hierarchical Tucker tensor decomposition (hTTD) to compress network parameters without compromising accuracy. Concurrently, we developed a hardware architecture specifically optimized for the hTTD structure. To manage on-chip memory limits during inference, we implemented an efficient processing network (PN) architecture and an access optimized-hTTD (AOhTTD) format. Evaluation across video datasets, including MSRC-V1, UIUC, YouTube-Actions, and UCF-101, demonstrates that our compressed H.264-encoded LSTM model achieves near-identical accuracy to its uncompressed counterpart. Furthermore, our hardware design supporting the AOhTTD architecture delivers a 50x improvement in operations per byte (OP/B) compared to existing state-of-the-art tensor decomposition hardware. Finally, simulations utilizing the UCF-101 dataset confirm that our algorithm and hardware co-designed for H.264 LSTM networks surpass traditional designs in on-chip memory efficiency, computational speed, and overall energy consumption. The proposed algorithm and hardware architecture for H.264 AOhTTD networks are open-sourced at: https://github.com/CSU-NLP/TTD_H.264_Access_Optimized_Network. Additionally, an architecture for lossless hierarchical Tucker decomposition (LHTD) videos in the raw domain is available at: https://github.com/CSU-NLP/LHTD_Architecture. These contributions offer valuable references for both algorithmic and hardware developments in hierarchical Tucker decomposition (HTD) networks.

Odoni established that for fields of characteristic zero, the Galois group of the $n$-th iterate of the generic monic polynomial of degree $d \geq 2$ corresponds to the $n$-fold iterated wreath product of the symmetric group $S_d$, a result later generalized to positive characteristic by Juul. In this work, we consider a finite field $\F_q$ where $q$ is a power of a prime $p > 2$, and let $k = \overline{\F}_q$ denote its algebraic closure. We demonstrate that for any irreducible monic polynomial $F(t,x) \in k[t][x]$ of degree $n > 0$ which is separable over $k(t)$, and a generic monic polynomial $\Phi(a_0,\dots,a_{d-1},t)$ in $t$ of degree $d \geq 2$ with algebraically independent coefficients $\mathbf a = (a_0,\dots,a_{d-1})$, the Galois group of the $m$-th iterate of the composite polynomial $F(t,\Phi(\mathbf a,t))$ over $k(a_0,\dots,a_{d-1})$ is the $m$-fold iterated wreath product of $S_{nd}$. Furthermore, applying this finding to an explicit form of the Chebotarev density theorem for function fields yields analogues of the Bateman-Horn conjecture and Chowla's conjecture regarding the autocorrelation of the Möbius function, particularly as the finite field grows large; these applications are detailed herein. Additionally, we prove an analogue of Schinzel's hypothesis H for the primality of iterates of composites of a product of linear polynomials over finite fields, which enables us to construct counterexamples to the arithmetic analogues of the above applications. These counterexamples arise from an iterated extension of a finite field $\F_r$, where $r$ is a power of a prime $p$ dividing four times the number of times each such linear polynomial appears in said product. Finally, we sketch how these results can be adapted for the case of an algebraically closed field of characteristic 2. The notation $S_n$ represents the symmetric group on $n$ elements, and $S_n^{(m)}$ denotes its $m$-fold iterated wreath product.

This paper examines the Schrödinger equation featuring a mass-supercritical focusing nonlinearity in the region outside a smooth, compact, convex obstacle in $\R^{d}$, subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions. We demonstrate that solutions possessing negative energy exhibit finite-time blow-up. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is energy-subcritical and given further symmetry constraints, we establish blow-up governed by the same optimal ground-state criterion found in Holmer and Roudenko's work on $\R^{d}$. The traditional Glassey proof, which relies on the concavity of variance, is inapplicable in the presence of an obstacle due to boundary terms arising in the second derivative of the variance that carry an unfavorable sign. To address this, our primary approach involves introducing a novel modified variance that is bounded from below and strictly concave for the specific solutions under consideration. Conversely, boundary terms play a constructive role in our concentration compactness argument; specifically, they facilitate the global existence proof by enabling the application of Strichartz estimates in the exterior domain. Ultimately, we derive the explicit blow-up profile in the sense of Lemariy-Rieuge profiles within the geometric optics approximation.

Hypothesis testing is a fundamental component of cognitive science, with Bayes factors offering a primary method for evaluating hypotheses based on their compatibility with observed data to facilitate selection among competing models. Although Bayes factors provide a direct approach to hypothesis evaluation, they are notably sensitive to specific data characteristics and model assumptions. Furthermore, their practical application remains uncertain regarding its robustness to data anomalies and the precision required for eliciting prior distributions of likelihood parameters. This study examines the utility of Bayesian methods for analyzing potentially problematic data within cognitive science. We demonstrate that workflow techniques, originally developed for hypothesis evaluation in physics, can be effectively adapted for cognitive science. Additionally, we utilize these workflows to clarify the interpretation of Bayes factors when dealing with outliers, while emphasizing the necessity of carefully specifying prior distributions for likelihood parameters. Finally, we apply these workflows to evaluate the U-scan algorithm, a method designed for detecting outliers in cognitive science data. The results indicate that U-scores lack informativeness for individual data points and fail to account for the influence of multiple outliers on posterior inferences. Overall, workflow techniques for assessing Bayes factors offer a valuable framework for scrutinizing statistical analyses in cognitive science, particularly when data may be flawed or when prior elicitation involves complexity. Ultimately, these approaches promote greater accountability in statistical modeling and support more informed decisions when utilizing Bayes factors. Discourse markers, such as {\it by contrast} and {\it happily}, are words or phrases that indicate semantic and/or pragmatic connections between clauses or sentences. Recent studies have productively investigated predicting discourse markers between sentence pairs to derive accurate sentence representations beneficial for various classification tasks. This paper adopts a different approach: we utilize a model trained to predict discourse markers between sentence pairs to infer plausible markers for pairs with known semantic relations (sourced from existing classification datasets). These inferences enable us to examine the relationship between discourse markers and the semantic relations annotated in these datasets. Although handcrafted mappings have been suggested between markers and discourse relations for limited sets of markers and categories, hundreds of discourse markers express a diverse range of relations, and there is no agreed-upon taxonomy of relations among competing theories (which are predominantly constructed top-down). By employing an automatic prediction method over existing semantically annotated datasets, we offer a bottom-up characterization of discourse markers in English. The resulting dataset, called DiscSense, is publicly accessible. Using this dataset, we define a metric to assess the specificity of discourse markers toward a sentence's semantic relation. Our analysis of DiscSense reveals that some markers are highly selective regarding a sentence's labeled relation, whereas others are less so. Furthermore, we identify that existing discourse relation categories in these datasets might not fully align with the discourse relations actually conveyed by the marker pairs and context, as evidenced by the low specificity of certain context and marker combinations for a sentence's labeled relation. Finally, based on the characteristics of our dataset, we propose potential research directions for future studies using DiscSense. Extensive experiments validate the utility of our dataset and metric for predicting and generating discourse markers given a sentence's semantic relation. Our analysis underscores the value of integrating linguistic theories of context types with machine learning methods over large, automatically generated datasets to derive robust conclusions. To facilitate this, we introduce simple, practical methods for representing contexts (i.e., context + relation) and for predicting the type of context. We introduce the concept of multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics to substantially decrease the number of focal plane detectors required for wide-field X-ray monitors using lobster-eye (LE) technology. In this MuLE setup, a single LE mirror is partitioned into multiple segments, directing X-rays reflected from each segment onto one image sensor within a multiplexed arrangement. When each LE segment is oriented at a distinct rotation angle, the azimuthal rotation of the reconstructed cross-like image from a point source allows for the identification of the specific segment responsible for focusing the X-rays onto the imager. Utilizing a 30 cm focal length and 10 x 10 cm^2 LE segments, a field of view covering approximately 1 steradian can be achieved with 36 segments and just four imagers (each with a total area of 10 x 10 cm^2). Ray tracing simulations were conducted to assess a nine-segment MuLE configuration. These simulations indicated that for a 100-second transient, the flux corresponding to a 5-sigma detection limit between 0.5 and 2 keV would be approximately 2 x 10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1 (10 mCrab). Furthermore, the simulations demonstrated that the direction of transients with fluxes ranging from 14 to 17 mCrab at 0.6 keV could be determined with 99.7% confidence. We conclude that the MuLE configuration has the potential to serve as an effective on-board instrument for small satellites dedicated to future X-ray wide-field transient monitoring.

Our findings indicate that incorporating velocity information alongside the density field yields negligible improvements when utilizing Gaussian Convolutional kernels. However, when employing deconvolutional kernels to reconstruct halo mass from the density field alone, the model struggles to account for small-scale fluctuations, resulting in underestimations of $M_{\text{collapse}}$ and a leftward shift in the predicted halo mass distribution. Detecting magnetic fields with high sensitivity remains a significant challenge in metrology. In this study, we introduce a Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry setup designed to measure extremely weak local magnetic fields expelled by a superconductor—acting as a "testing magnet"—via the Meissner effect. The resulting magnetic field gradient near the superconductor generates a centripetal acceleration on the atoms within the interferometer, enabling detection through atomic interference patterns. Building on the fact that gravitational acceleration of atoms has been measured with a precision of $10^{-12}$ g, the sensitivity of this method for detecting the expelled local field could potentially reach $10^{-14}$ T. To verify this approach, we constructed a prototype and successfully identified the local field gradient by measuring the centripetal acceleration of atoms caused by a 100-nT field in a bulk lead superconductor cooled to 7.2 K. This demonstration confirms that atomic interferometry can sense local magnetic fields as weak as approximately 100 nT. Such sensitivity is sufficient to detect the intrinsic magnetic field of a YBCO (Yttrium Barium Copper Oxide) superconductor when cooled below its critical temperature. If this feasibility is validated, an atom interferometer could serve as a compact, high-sensitivity magnetometer capable of identifying magnetic field enhancements in materials by as much as a factor of 100 below 90 K with potential high precision. Furthermore, this technique offers a straightforward means to directly and locally test Marx's prediction of the London magnetic field inside a superconductor. Other potential applications include precisely determining the London penetration depth and providing direct local evidence for the magnetic field exclusion mechanism in Josephson junctions. Additionally, this method could directly verify the local magnetic field expulsion in amorphous metal ribbons, thereby directly confirming the magnetic field exclusion in the flux-trapping phenomenon. To achieve the highest possible sensitivity when detecting the intrinsic field of a YBCO sample, future work should focus on minimizing the atomic interferometer's vertical acceleration and maximizing the length of its arms. Ultimately, this could enable the detection of local magnetic field changes in YBCO as small as 0.1 mT with a precision approaching $10^{-5}$ (0.01 T). Finally, this approach provides a direct local test of Marx's prediction, complementing recent efforts that utilized SQUIDs (Superconducting Quantum Interference Devices) to indirectly detect such fields in a YBCO Josephson junction.

We introduce a fully relativistic, first-principles theoretical framework designed to calculate the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities situated on superconducting surfaces, thereby establishing a material-specific methodology for analyzing Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states. Through a detailed examination of an Mn adatom and two configurations of Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface, we offer comprehensive descriptions of their local electronic and orbital structures, as well as the specific superconducting states responsible for observed YSR features. Notably, our model reveals that spin-flipped quasiparticle excitations exhibit significant local character, contrasting with recent interpretations that attribute these excitations to bulk-like mechanisms. Furthermore, our theoretical spectra align closely with recent experimental data, resolving discrepancies between theory and practice regarding y*-like excitations and the spectral features of the y+ YSR state. This framework of "impurity Green's function" calculations serves as a potent investigative tool for exploring localized electronic states at material-specific surfaces, potentially facilitating the design of novel qubit-like magnetic impurity states for quantum information applications. Ultimately, our analysis indicates that the splitting of y+ and y*-like excitations in the YSR states of a Mn derived triplet configuration is driven by distinct resonant behaviors between spin-up and spin-down quasiparticle excitations.

This report outlines the methodologies that secured 3rd and 4th place in tasks 1 and 2, respectively, at the ISIC 2019 challenge, which aims to diagnose skin cancer using images and metadata. Although the dataset contains nine classes, one is an outlier and absent from the actual data. To address this, we employed an ensemble of 11 convolutional neural networks (CNNs), developing two specific strategies for the missing outlier class: an entropy-based post-processing approach and a meta-learner method. We detail these methodologies and their hyperparameters, which were manually tuned to balance validation accuracy with model complexity, achieving high scores on standard challenge metrics. Furthermore, we introduced an automatic tuning approach capable of replicating our results without manual intervention. Our frameworks are accessible via https://github.com/SeeBye/AI-ISIC-19 and will be executed on challenge data during the event. It is important to note that while our solutions prioritize accuracy, they may not be directly applicable to real-world medical scenarios, as such deployments would require methods ensuring class fairness and robustness against adversarial attacks or distribution shifts. Future work should specifically target the integration of the outlier class into automated production systems for clinical use. (This abstract was written by a student. We bring together Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem (1931), Tarski's Undefinability Theorem (1933), Godel-Carnap's Diagonal Lemma (1934), and Rosser's Incompleteness Theorem (1936), which strengthens Godel's first result. These proofs share significant similarities, yet existing presentations are scattered, often lacking unified notation or structural clarity. Our goal is to offer a streamlined, unified treatment of these four landmark theorems of mathematical logic. Additionally, we provide a simplified proof of the simplification proposed by Smullyan (1992) to Godel's first incompleteness theorem.

Invariant manifolds constitute crucial sets within the stability analysis of dynamical systems. This paper offers a concise overview of invariant sets, presenting findings on the existence of invariant lines and parabolas within planar polynomial systems. Additionally, we establish the criteria required for linear subspaces to remain invariant in fractional-order systems. Furthermore, we highlight a significant result demonstrating that, aside from linear subspaces, no other invariant manifolds exist in such fractional-order systems. These conclusions carry important implications for the stability study of systems modeled using fractional-order dynamics. It is anticipated that these findings will guide researchers in investigating the dynamical behavior of specific fractional-order models. Regarding methodology, our proofs rely primarily on the definition of fractional-order derivatives and their fundamental properties, notably that a positive constant is the only function whose Caputo derivative is zero. This approach avoids reliance on complex numerical simulations or specific fractional calculus models, ensuring the results hold universally across all definitions of fractional derivatives. Consequently, these findings are applicable to systems described by Caputo, Riemann-Liouville, or other fractional derivative operators. These conclusions also remain valid under alternative definitions of stability for fractional-order systems, including those proposed in [14] and [25].

This study addresses the inverse problem of identifying a source term within a structural acoustic PDE model, which consists of a two- or three-dimensional interior acoustic wave equation linked to a Kirchhoff plate equation via a boundary interface. For this system, we establish uniqueness and derive stability estimates for the source term using a single boundary measurement of the "structure." The uniqueness proof relies on Carleman estimates, while the stability result is achieved through an observability inequality combined with a compactness/uniqueness argument. Finally, an operator theoretic approach provides the necessary regularity for the initial conditions to attain the desired stability estimate. The practical application of this theory is demonstrated via a numerical example that identifies an unknown source from simulated data. In that context, the boundary referred to for the source identification is not necessarily the one connecting the acoustic and structural components, nor does it have to be a physical boundary. Regarding the inverse problem's setup, we do not assume knowledge of the material parameters defining the plate's dynamics. While prior work has solved similar issues for a specific boundary shape (a circle) with known material constants, our analysis requires no such assumptions, rendering our result novel even when the material parameters are known.

This study examines the coherence of electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino behavior, and dark matter properties within the minimal scoto-seesaw framework. By extending the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw with the minimal dark sector, we establish a physical mechanism for neutrino oscillation lengths: the atmospheric mass scale originates from tree-level seesaw dynamics, whereas the solar scale emerges radiatively through mediation by the dark sector. We pinpoint parameter regions that satisfy theoretical constraints, align with dark matter relic density, and are viable under direct detection limits. Employing two-loop renormalization group equations, we investigate vacuum stability and the consistency of the fundamental dark parity symmetry, while also deriving a lower bound for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude. Our analysis reveals that the dark parity symmetry can remain valid only up to a scale of approximately $10^{12}$ GeV. Within this framework, the minimal dark force operates as a mixture of $U(1)_Y$ and $U(1)_D$, yielding a dark matter annihilation cross section of $\sim 10^{-24}\,\text{cm}^3\,\text{s}^{-1}$ and a resulting relic density determined by the balance between Higgs portal couplings and right-handed neutrino Yukawa couplings. To explore direct detection phenomenology, we derived analytic expressions for electron scattering cross sections mediated by $Z$, $Z_D$, and Higgs exchanges. These interactions are too weak to be observed by current generation detectors, necessitating the use of next-generation experiments such as nCTA or PICO-1000 to test this model. Finally, we assessed the feasibility of generating the cosmic baryon asymmetry via thermal leptogenesis, concluding that while the necessary conditions for leptogeneses are met, the cross section for freeze-out to achieve the correct relic density is insufficient, requiring an alternative mechanism such as resonant seesaw-induced right-handed neutrino decay.
